item.title: The Triumph of Maxxing, a Suffix with a Superpower
item.description:
Media

The Triumph of Maxxing, a Suffix with a Superpower

'Looksmaxxing' is everywhere—but where did it come from?

Posted July 8, 2026

Maxxing has become unavoidable online
Source: Grok / xAI

What is looksmaxxing, and why are so many people talking about it?

A good definition of the term can be found in one of the first articles to describe it: "Enhancing one's sex appeal through weight lifting, skin and hair treatments and even plastic surgery" (Brennan, 2020).

Although self-improvement is hardly a new phenomenon, the suffix from this term, -maxxing, has taken on a life of its own. Tracing its origin, as well as the way it has attached itself to so many other terms, tells us a great deal about where new words are coming from—and whether we'll still be using them in a year or two.

An Origin Story

Maxxing seems to have originated in gaming culture in the late 1990s; it appears in terms like min-maxing, in which players attempt to balance good and bad traits or outcomes.

Looksmaxxing itself, however, seems to have bubbled up from online manosphere culture and is most closely associated with misogynistic incel 4chan and Reddit postings dating from the mid-2010s.

The most prominent contemporary advocate of looksmaxxing is the online influencer Clavicular, Braden Peters, who has advocated softmaxxing (improving one’s appearance through better grooming, skin care, or better nutrition). And more controversially, via hardmaxxing, which includes injections of growth hormone, cosmetic surgery, and even bone smashing. Psychology Today has run several posts about the dangers of hardmaxxing.

However, looksmaxxing can also be found in subreddits like r/Splendida, dating from early 2021. This forum was created as “an exclusive space for women to discuss objective beauty. Posts are based on science, research, experiences and anecdotes.” The concept of looksmaxxing, in its various guises, has been pursued by men and women alike.

Maxxing as a Viral Meme

Ideas or memes that spread online are often compared with viruses, which can lurk in a host in a dormant state for long periods before suddenly “going viral.” This analogy seems particularly apt to explain the career of looksmaxxing.

Although the term had existed for several years before this, a LexisNexis search identifies its first appearance in a mainstream publication in December of 2018. The British weekly paper The Sunday Times quoted a man in his mid-thirties as saying, “I will keep on looksmaxxing [because] I want a better life for myself" (Wiseman, 2018).

But the term would not appear in The New York Times until nearly two years later, in an article about British orthodontists. It was also during this period that the term became popular on TikTok.

Tracking the appearance of looksmaxxing in The New York Times proves instructive. Its journalists and opinion columnists have used it 44 times total. Before 2024, the term appeared in just three articles. In 2024, it made five appearances, and then in 2025, there were six sightings. But during the first half of 2026, it appeared no less than 30 times. Clearly, the spring of 2026 was the point at which looksmaxxing went viral and crossed into the linguistic mainstream.

A Productive Term?

Clearly, looksmaxxing is having a moment. But will its viral suffix spread and infect hundreds of other words?

Suffix particles do have a way of becoming a regular part of the language. A good example is -gate, used to denote scandal. It originated in the Watergate affair of 1972-'73, with the eponymous hotel standing in for a variety of misdeeds perpetrated by the Nixon administration.

The term was first used generically—and ironically—in 1973 by The National Lampoon. Since then, however, it has been applied to hundreds of episodes, from the trivial to the consequential.

Similarly, -washing has become a conventional way of describing something done in a secret or duplicitous way. Derived from whitewashing, it was first used in the mid-1980s, when greenwashing was coined—it refers to corporations that falsely portray themselves as environmentally conscious. Since then, virtually all the shades of the rainbow have been used to describe similar behaviors.

If we employ a productivity criterion to evaluate the success of maxxing, it does seem to have spawned many new terms, mostly in the context of optimization. During June alone, outlets like The New York Times, the British newspaper The Observer, and various Substack columns ran stories mentioning birthmaxxing, bodymaxxing, doommaxxing, humanmaxxing, mindmaxxing, and even penis-maxxing and spermmaxxing (don’t ask).

Shortly before the conflict with Iran began in February 2026, the Pentagon tweeted about lethalitymaxxing, and at the Oscars the following month, Conan O’Brien joked about host-maxxing. But whether any of these coinages will stand the test of time is an open question.

A Suffix with Staying Power?

Have we achieved peak maxxing? It’s not at all unusual for a new word or suffix to take the language by storm and then fade into obscurity.

This has been the fate of many similar particles, like -ville to refer to a particular quality (think squaresville or dullsville) or -palooza (derived from lollapalooza) to refer to a special or large-scale event, as in food-palooza or shopping-palooza. Both of these suffixes had their moment in the sun before fading away and are now ironically used as a throwback to an earlier time when they were popular.

And how useful is maxxing, anyway? There's almost always a simple way to express the same idea. Instead of saying "I'm bookmaxxing," for example, one can just as easily say they're binge-reading.

Maxxing may be everywhere right now, but it soon may be only a memory—an ephemeral bit of slang from the mid-2020s.

item.title: What the Pursuit of Happiness Really Means
item.description:
Happiness

What the Pursuit of Happiness Really Means

It's about doing good, not feeling good.

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • Happiness is about doing good, not feeling good.
  • Happiness is active, not passive.
  • Happiness is not selfish.

The Declaration of Independence names “the pursuit of happiness” as an unalienable right, alongside life and liberty. By including the pursuit of happiness, Thomas Jefferson altered John Locke’s claim that men have a right to life, liberty, and property.[1]

Jefferson followed George Mason in doing so. Mason included the phrase “pursuing and obtaining happiness” in the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776), and Jefferson heavily drew on this document in drafting the Declaration. There are many competing explanations for why he did so.

Including the “pursuit of happiness” may have been a simple rhetorical flourish because it creates an ennobling picture of government.[2] John Adams remarked that Jefferson had a gift of writing and “peculiar felicity of expression.”[3] Another account is that Jefferson removed “property” because he wanted to avoid perpetuating the property ownership of slaves.[4]

A third explanation is that this phrase accords with natural law—the classical idea that there are moral truths in nature, which are discoverable by reason. Central to this philosophy is the human aim at a flourishing or happy life, which “whether conscious and explicit or not, is the universal occupation and preoccupation of mankind.”[5] By affirming the pursuit of happiness as an unalienable right, the Declaration affirms the government’s intention to support the flourishing of its citizens.

American Happiness in Decline

By many measures, American happiness is in decline. According to the 2026 World Happiness Report, the United States ranks twenty-third globally for happiness, following a trend of recent declines among Western industrial countries.[6] Much of the decline of happiness is attributed to heavy social media use, in addition to declining social institutions, loneliness, and the erosion of public trust.[7]

If the pursuit of happiness is an unalienable right, we might wonder why many people seem to be alienated from it. Additionally, we might wonder what the Founders meant by happiness. Did they conceive of happiness the way we tend to think of it today? The short answer is no.

Their conception of happiness, shaped by classical thinkers such as Plato, Aristotle, and Cicero, was as follows:

1. Happiness Is About Doing Good, Not Feeling Good [8]

Today we often conceive of happiness in hedonic, or pleasure-seeking terms—as feeling good, instead of doing good. We equate happiness with smiley faces and good feelings. But there are limitations to this view.

Sometimes we take pleasure in the wrong things. An example is schadenfreude, or “harm-joy”—satisfaction in the suffering of another. Also, happy feelings are ephemeral. Sometimes I feel happy at breakfast, then I feel sad that I have to answer an email, then I see the nice weather and feel happy again, until I get into my car and experience traffic and feel annoyed. Feelings can offer important information about the world around us, but they tell us very little about the quality of our lives.

Additionally, many of the least smiley-face moments in a person’s life also tend to be the most meaningful. Consider raising children, which is quite challenging, but can be an important part of a good life. Also consider climbing a mountain or running a marathon. Marathons are often a “frown parade.”[9] There are very few smiles, yet people often say that running marathons and partaking in other arduous goods is part of a happy life. A good life and a pleasant life are not the same thing.

2. Happiness Is Active, Not Passive

In “Happiness as Achievement,” Julia Annas shares an anecdote about business school students. They were asked whether, if they discovered a large sum of money, their lives would be happy thereafter. The students overwhelmingly said no. It is not that money does not matter. Of course it matters so we can meet our material needs. However, the students were convinced that striving and effort are part of a good life. Happiness is not passively received.[10]

Aristotle defines happiness as an “activity of the soul in accordance with virtue.”[11] It involves choosing and acting. It consists of striving for virtue (excellence), rather than passively receiving things. This active character of happiness is consistent with contemporary positive psychology. Martin Seligman reports that factors within one’s voluntary control, including habit-formation—which can require “real effort”—has significant and enduring impacts on happiness.[12]

3. Happiness Is Not Selfish

This semester, I taught a class on the pursuit of happiness. One assignment was for students to select a contemporary self-help book, discern how the author defined happiness, and place this definition in conversation with happiness as conceived of by the American Founders. Was the view compatible with a flourishing American citizenry?

In almost every case, my students responded no. A common reason why was that they found the perspectives to be self-centered and insular in ways that were incompatible with the Founders’ views of human nature. They challenged the idea that a person could self-actualize or become their "best self" by putting their own interests first and neglecting care of neighbors or duties of citizenship. We are social animals. According to the classical thinkers informing the Founders, this was a natural fact about us as human beings. Thus, flourishing is not an individual equation. It involves other people.

item.title: Exploring the Neglect of Athletes Being Human and its Impact
item.description:
Sport and Competition

Exploring the Neglect of Athletes Being Human and its Impact

The damage coaches and parents create when disregarding basic people elements

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • Coaches and parents are often dismissive of the human factor of young athletes.
  • Too much practicing is often doing more harm than good.
  • Ignoring athletes' freedom of choice in what they're doing is depriving them of a human need.
  • Threat and fear are dominant experiences for many athletes in today's toxic youth sports culture.
The failure to take into account that athletes are human beings is detrimental to mental health as well as performance.performance a
Source: AI-generated photo by Gemini.

The human factor.

That’s something that many mentors and leaders in all realms, including sports, ignore in their dealings with people.

The focus herein is on the coaches, trainers, and parents—within a sports context—who often overlook that athletes are human beings, too. It’s a miscue that can lead to a crash-and-burn for everyone involved.

While their efforts may be well-intentioned, coaches, parents, and others in the sports and performance world often fail to recognize the destructive nature of what they are doing.

Let’s explore the elements of those damaging efforts and a few simple solutions.

Too Much Training

Many coaches and parents believe that more, more, more practice is better, better, better. Wrong! When dealing with humans, less is often more.

Research conducted by Ericsson, Krampe, & Tesch-Romer (1993), The Role of Deliberate Practice in the Acquisition of Expert Performance, demonstrates that humans can only endure one hour of intense and sustained individualized practice. Due to physical and mental exhaustion, any more than that will likely result in deteriorating performance and disdain for the coaches and parents who are coercing it. A collegiate golfer once shared that his coach instructed him to practice on a golf course during the team’s off-season for a minimum of seven to eight hours a day!

Team and group practices can run longer because they are less intensive and individualized; therefore, two-and-a-half- to three-hour sessions are fine.

Another thing modern-day youth coaches often do, which ignores the human factor (and that parents passively align with), is demand year-round, coached practice. Contrast that with professional teams that get months off from regimented training when the season ends. Many youth and high school athletes are forced to devote themselves to year-round training with minimal time off.

What happens with such forced, elongated commitment? Burnout and distaste for a sport the athlete once loved and enjoyed. It’s like this. Think of your favorite food. Imagine what would happen if you ate it almost every day of the year. You’d probably get tired of it.

Another negative outcome of too much practice is overuse injuries. That’s another story for another time.

Spending too much time on a sport also interferes with having a full, meaningful life. Human beings are much more than athletes. They have families, jobs, school, and friends. Athletes also possess other interests that are all neglected and damaged by obsessive devotion to a sport.

Overdevoted athletes are also deprived of opportunities to discover other passions and talents hidden inside them. They are not living a full life.

That’s what happens when the human factor is ignored!

Simple solution: Less can be more. Shorten practice sessions and give athletes adequate time off between seasons.

Forced and Coerced Training

What if you were not only eating your favorite food every day, but were being forced to? When asked that question, most people say they would lose their appetite for that food and come to despise it, not to mention resent the person(s) forcing it.

The human need for choice is ignored.

That’s another aspect of the human factor that coaches and parents dismiss. They don’t recognize how they are deflating the performer’s passion for their sport and harming the relationship between the athlete and the people who are not allowing choice.

Many of those coaches and parents are influenced by the “10,000-hour” rule, popularized by Malcolm Gladwell in his book, Outliers (2011). It’s based on the results of the Ericsson et al. study that found that elite performers had invested 10,000-plus hours of devoted practice and training in a specialized sport to achieve their elite status.

The 10,000-hour rule, however, has been badly misunderstood. That will be detailed later on.

Simple solution: Allow athletes more choices in their sport endeavors.

Unrealistic Expectations

Another coaching behavior that is dismissive of the human factor and partly fueled by a misunderstanding of the 10,000-hour rule is leading athletes and parents to believe that a college athletic scholarship or professional career will happen if they put in enough practice time.

Given that only 6 to 10 percent of high school athletes receive college athletic scholarships and a much smaller percentage reach the professional level, it’s a scam to be pushing such a belief. Yet many young people and their parents buy into it, creating an unrealistic expectation that only creates pressure, long-term disappointment, and potential devastation when those expectations don’t materialize.

Some coaches and sports administrators promote those false expectations because they believe that it will motivate athletes to work harder and make their team better. Some do it to market their youth sports business and coaching reputation. All that ignores the negative impact it could have, once again dismissive of the human factor.

The Ericsson et al. research explains that the intensive practice and specialization in one sport, as described in the 10,000-hour rule, is a personal, independent choice—not the coach’s or the parents’—based on the athlete’s personal desire and self-recognized talent. Athletes don’t have the maturity and experience to make such an independent, well-founded decision until the age of 16 at the earliest, according to Ericsson’s findings.

Simple solution: Allow the athlete to decide to commit to focus on one sport with intense training.

The Net Effect

Threat of a failed sports career if they don’t practice enough. Fear of getting cut, losing playing time, or getting in trouble if they don’t adhere to the unrealistic year-round time demands of a coach, and dropping out of other activities to specialize in one sport.

The threat and fear that they’ll be letting their parents down if they don’t get a college scholarship after all the time and money invested in their attempt to reach that expectation.

Fear of identity loss, due to a life and future that has been entirely defined by sports.

Threat and fear can work in the short run. It can motivate us to study for an exam, but that sort of motivation for something intended for enjoyment can lead to loss of interest, burnout, and quitting.

Sustained motivation comes from a desire and hunger for what you’re doing. Imagine how excited you’d be to devour a food or sport you hadn’t tasted in months.

“Freedom” and “relief.” That’s how many athletes express their experience when they are finally released from the threat and fear of today’s youth sport culture upon leaving the sport. It’s as if they’ve been locked up since they began playing, and now they’ve escaped imprisonment.

Simple solution: Erase the threat and fear by lowering forced time demands and enabling freedom of choice.

Enable the human factor.

item.title: How Embodied Regulation Helps When Words Fail
item.description:
Sensory Processing Disorder

How Embodied Regulation Helps When Words Fail

My daughter's sensory processing challenges changed the way I approached emotional dysregulation.

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • Most patients report some benefits from talk therapy, but verbal regulation isn't enough for some.
  • Sensory processing disorder, a brain difference that triggers hyper- or hyposensitivity, may help explain why.
  • Alternative therapies are becoming more popular as more people seek embodied approaches to healing.
Source: Photo by Volodymyr Hryshchenko on Unsplash

Around 75 percent of patients report positive benefits from psychotherapy. That’s great, unless you’re in the other 25 percent.

Sometimes talking isn’t enough—and the thing that really brought this lesson home for me was learning about my daughter’s sensory processing difference. Before her evaluation, I thought sensory processing disorder was either just a comorbidity of autism and ADHD or just a personal preference, kind of like being a highly sensitive person or not liking cilantro.

Turns out I was wrong.

What to Know About Sensory Processing Disorder

Sensory processing disorder is an actual brain difference. Brain scans have shown that white matter in the back of the brain is abnormal in children with sensory processing disorder.

This means their brain wiring causes them to be either overly sensitive or under sensitive. Sounds, sights, tastes, smells, or sensations can trigger children with sensory processing disorder, or they may be underresponsive to one or more of these senses.

My daughter freaks out if her clothes feel funny, if anything smells funny, or if she’s too hot. It’s no laughing matter. She can become so dysregulated that it takes hours to calm her down.

My initial reaction to her discomfort and dysregulation was to try to talk her out of it, to rationalize with her. “Your socks aren’t that bad.” “It’s hot in the summertime.” “You’re a big girl now; you can manage.”

I felt powerless to help her and stuck in my verbal ways. Talking is often our first reaction. We do it often and not always thoughtfully.

Lessons from Sensory Processing Differences: Why Embodied Regulation Makes Such a Difference

After they evaluated my daughter, and the term sensory processing disorder started being thrown around, I did some reading. I read The Out of Sync Child by Carol Stock Kranowitz and Sensational Kids by Lucy Jane Miller, and I started trying to implement some of the occupational therapy strategies at home.

I started pressing a vibrating pillow on my daughter when she got upset, instead of lecturing or processing. I had her jump on the bed when I noticed she was getting agitated, instead of telling her to calm down. We pushed on each other’s hands and did wheelbarrows around the house.

I was surprised at how much more connected I felt to her. She didn’t need any words because sometimes words fail us, or we're just not ready to hear them.

Think about how many times you’re dysregulated and not ready for words. When I’m upset, I don’t typically want to hear about why I shouldn’t be or how I should feel something else. Instead, I might want some silent company or an understanding hug.

Sometimes, we're all a little talked out. The verbal parts of our brain only take us so far. There’s a whole embodied world inside all of us that craves more than conversation. We need touch, connection, eye contact, and activity.

Maybe that’s why alternative therapies like EMDR and psychedelic-assisted therapy are gaining prominence. Talking is just one small fraction of who we are. Unlocking the rest requires a different kind of connection—an embodied connection that can tell us so much more.

item.title: When Your Partner Is Experiencing Erection Difficulty
item.description:
Sex

When Your Partner Is Experiencing Erection Difficulty

How to support and process the experience of erectile dysfunction.

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • Erection difficulty is often about more than just attraction.
  • Process your emotions before trying to problem-solve.
  • Talk about it outside of the bedroom.
  • Focus on non-penetrative pleasure to lower the pressure.

You’ve started to notice your partner has had difficulty maintaining erections. He isn’t saying much about it, but you can tell he’s bothered—he apologizes, he ends the intimacy, maybe he even starts avoiding sex.

You’re upset, too. You were looking forward to a moment of pleasure and connection that just abruptly ended. You want to help your partner but aren’t sure how. Sex starts to feel tense or stressful. Worry develops that he’s no longer attracted to you or that he’s seeking attention elsewhere.

All of this is common in couples navigating erectile problems. That doesn’t mean it’s easy. Whether you are the wife, husband, short-term partner, or long-time love, you want help—for your partner, yourself, and your relationship.

The following case is a composite with client details anonymized to protect privacy.

Source: Ketut Subiyanto / Pexels

Mel and Dave had been together for three years. They had infrequent sex throughout their relationship, but rationalized it was due to living apart. After two years, they moved in together. Dave began experiencing erectile problems, and their sex life dwindled further. Mel worried, “Is it me?”

It’s Probably Not You

Sometimes, erection loss does occur in relationships because of a loss of attraction. But that is not always the case and doesn’t need to be your first assumption. When we personalize the problem, that’s just the mind looking for security and control.

Erection difficulty can happen for all manner of reasons, some of which may involve you, some may not. The body and mind are not always in sync. A man can be in love with his partner, feel desire, be turned on, and still have trouble with erections.

You are probably not the cause of your partner’s erectile issues, but you may have a role in how they are navigated.

Mel didn’t realize the pressure they were unintentionally adding. Questions and comments like, “What’s wrong?” or “You’ve never had this problem before” were meant to nudge Dave toward a solution but instead echoed his self-criticism.

When Mel got tired of trying, resentment came out in frustrated sighs, which further discouraged Dave. Both of them felt sad and alone.

Your Emotions Are Valid

You don’t have to hide your feelings or be relentlessly reassuring. Silence can feel like rejection; pure optimism can feel dismissive. Your genuine experience is important—it’s what connects you. If you’re upset, that’s worth sharing when emotions are not running high. When tension disrupts intimacy, you both might need a break to cool down. Be intentional about how you come back together.

If you’re feeling sad in the moment, it’s okay to ask for comfort. Your partner may want the same thing. The grief and frustration are usually about more than just your partner’s erections. What do they mean to you? Validation? Connection? Consider processing with a therapist—they can help you identify unconscious expectations.

Talking to Him

The moment erection loss happens is not the time for problem-solving. Have that conversation at a calmer time.

If your partner isn’t initiating a conversation about his erections, start with a gentle observation: “I’ve noticed you’ve been having some difficulty maintaining erections, and I’m curious what you’ve been feeling.” Once he starts sharing, validate his experience. Acknowledge any stress or embarrassment.

Share your own feelings. “I feel sad when we don’t have intercourse. That’s one of the ways I feel close to you.” Or “I worry about your health and want to help.” Make these statements from a non-demanding stance. Frame them as “I” statements rather than starting with You. “You should__.” Or “Why don’t you__.” You are sharing your experience, not telling your partner what he has to fix. The intent is to invite collaboration.

From there, you can ask team questions. “How can we reduce pressure together?” “How can we address this outside of the bedroom?” Be patient. Medication, therapy, and behavioral changes all need time to work. Notice any expectations for quick results.

In the meantime, if difficulty occurs during sex, take a break or shift to non-penetrative touch. Avoid ending the intimacy abruptly. Direct your attention to what is possible instead of what isn’t happening.

Taking Penetrative Pressure Off

Erectile issues are often most challenging around penetrative sex. It’s a reinforcing problem: the expectation creates performance pressure, which negatively affects erections, which reaffirms the belief that sex is difficult. Taking intercourse off the table for a while and focusing on other forms of pleasure can break the cycle. It may not be easy—penetrative sex is often the default assumption or the preferred act. However, change won’t occur as long as you both hold onto old patterns.

Source: Mohammad Khoram / Pexels

Over several sessions, Mel accepted that he desired intimacy more often than Dave and learned that his low initiation wasn’t due to a lack of interest. When he knew that Mel’s initiations were not just about sex but physical closeness, he was likely to accept. That helped Mel get comfortable being the primary initiator.

During this time, Mel and Dave also agreed to focus on non-penetrative forms of pleasure in the short term. Even if Dave developed an erection, they would deprioritize intercourse.

Dave’s erections still waxed and waned, but how they navigated those moments changed. Instead of going silent, Dave asked to slow down. Instead of withdrawing into fear, Mel stayed present and focused on other sources of pleasure. Over time, they both panicked less, had more patience with each other, and got into the habit of checking in rather than assuming what the other was thinking or feeling.

That is the kind of shift that creates lasting change.

item.title: When Moving Goalposts Wear a Leader Down
item.description:
Leadership

When Moving Goalposts Wear a Leader Down

Why mission-driven leaders need closure, not just bigger goals.

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • Clear goals help leaders focus effort, but moving goalposts can make progress feel unfinished.
  • In mission-driven work, “more” can sound noble until it becomes “never enough.”
  • When success does not count, leaders can stay psychologically on the field even after the goal is reached.
  • Sustainable leadership means defining “enough” so they can stop, recover, and begin again.
Sustainable leadership means defining enough progress so leaders can stop, recover, and begin again.
Source: Jeff Frey / Used with permission

In one of my research interviews with a nonprofit leader, I heard a story that sounded familiar to anyone who has ever worked hard toward a goal only to watch the finish line move.

The organization had agreed on a goal. The plan was in motion, the teams were working, and they were on track to “beat the original goal by about 20 percent.”

Then someone with influence asked, “Why aren’t we doing more?”

There was no new number set… just the sense that the work already underway was somehow no longer enough. The leader described it like a football game:

“Imagine if you were playing a football game and you’re marching down the field… and then someone suddenly says, ‘Oh, no, it’s a two-hundred-yard field.’”

That was the feeling. The team had been getting closer to their goal, but suddenly they were no longer almost there. They were way behind. The leader described it as exhausting.

The Problem With “More”

In mission-driven work, “more” sounds noble. More people helped. More students reached. More patients served. More families supported. More impact created. “More” is a great goal.

But “more” becomes a problem when it’s “never enough.” A leader can watch the team hit the target, exceed expectations, and still feel as if the work failed because no one defined what “enough” would look like.

Research on goal setting has shown that specific, measurable, and achievable goals can improve motivation and performance. Goals help people focus attention, direct effort, and persist through difficulty (Locke & Latham, 2002). But goals work best when people know that what they are trying to accomplish is within reach.

A moving goalpost does not just change the target. It keeps the leader psychologically on the field.

Moving the Finish Line

There is an old idea in psychology called the goal-gradient effect. In simple terms, people often work harder as they feel themselves getting closer to a goal. You see it in loyalty programs, sporting events, fundraising campaigns, school assignments, and probably your own to-do list. When the end is in sight, energy rises.

That is why moving the finish line can feel so discouraging.

I see a version of this at home with my teenage boys. Some of their video games have levels. They work hard to finish the level, beat the boss, save their progress, and stop. There is a sense of progress and closure.

Other games are open-world. There is always one more thing to build, solve, explore, or conquer. Those games can be fun, but they also have a way of keeping my boys playing longer than they intended and pulling them back in after they’ve stopped because the work never feels fully done.

Mission-driven leadership can feel like the open-world version of work. The need is real, the mission matters, and there is always “more” that could be done.

That is exactly why leaders have to define closure.

When Success Still Feels Insufficient

The emotional problem is not ambition. Ambition can be healthy. Leaders should absolutely want themselves and their organizations to grow and improve.

The problem is when success doesn’t count.

When a leader or team is working toward a goal and hears “Why not more?” the organization may be teaching people that accomplishment is temporary and that there will always be another demand. Over time, that creates a culture where people stop trusting the goals themselves.

Researchers warn that goals can have side effects when they are “overused, too narrow, or disconnected from context” (Ordóñez, Schweitzer, Galinsky, & Bazerman, 2009). In real organizations, the danger is not usually the goal itself. It is what happens when the goal keeps growing beyond what is relevant to the plan, while the time, people, energy, and resources stay the same.

In mission-driven organizations, this can be especially hard to name because the work itself feels morally important. If the need is still there, how can we say we are done?

But “done for now” is not the same as “we stopped caring.”

The Cost of Unfinished Work

Unfinished work does not always stay at work.

Research suggests that unfinished goals can remain mentally active and interfere with other tasks, especially when there is no clear plan for what happens next (Masicampo & Baumeister, 2011). Work recovery research points in a similar direction: people need periods of psychological detachment from work to recover well, and leaders influence not only their own recovery but also the recovery norms of those around them (Sonnentag, 2019).

Moving goalposts not only create more work… they also create open loops.

Leaders go home still carrying the question: Are we succeeding? Did the goal change? Are we behind? What will be enough next time?

That kind of uncertainty is hard to put down.

Define Enough

Sustainable leadership does not mean refusing to grow, avoiding stretch goals, or ignoring new opportunities. It means refusing to confuse constant expansion with faithful leadership.

Leaders can still ask, “Should we do more? Can we serve more people? Is the original goal still the right goal?”

But those questions deserve a review process, not a vague request for “more.”

If the goal changes, name the change. If the target expands, explain why. If more is needed, identify the resources, trade-offs, and limits. And when the team reaches a meaningful milestone, stop long enough to acknowledge it for them and for yourself. Hold off on “more” until what is already in process is done; then begin a new project to accomplish it.

Why? Because leaders need closure too. Without it, every success feels short-lived, every milestone becomes just a stepping stone, and the leader never gets the psychological permission to stop. Closure is not laziness. It is what tells everyone that the goalposts have not moved.

To lead sustainably, define “enough” so you can stop, recover, and begin again.
